messages.content:
Two sentences, please: what is this passage about?

The building was of grey, lichen-blotched stone, with a high central portion and two curving wings, like the claws of a crab, thrown out on each side. In one of these wings the windows were broken and blocked with wooden boards, while the roof was partly caved in, a picture of ruin. The central portion was in little better repair, but the right-hand block was comparatively modern, and the blinds in the windows, with the blue smoke curling up from the chimneys, showed that this was where the family resided. Some scaffolding had been erected against the end wall, and the stone-work had been broken into, but there were no signs of any workmen at the moment of our visit. Holmes walked slowly up and down the ill-trimmed lawn and examined with deep attention the outsides of the windows.

The grey stone house has a tall middle and two curved wings, one of which is ruined and boarded up. The family lives in the newer right-hand part, and Holmes walks over the lawn studying the outside of the windows.

Please explain this to a young child in two or three sentences.

On the first cold morning of December, Rafiq's class at the government school was buzzing. "Yesterday a parrot flew into our class and said Miss's name!" Rafiq told Sarita Ma'am, who taught them English. "Remember, ma'am? It sat on the fan." The class laughed. "Rafiq, no parrot came," said a boy in front. Rafiq's face went red. "It did! It said good morning!" Sarita Ma'am thought for a moment. "The cartoon on the canteen TV yesterday, was there a talking parrot in it?" Rafiq opened his mouth, then closed it. "There was," he said slowly. "It sat on a fan." She nodded kindly. "Our brains mix up pictures sometimes. You weren't fibbing."

Rafiq told his teacher that a parrot flew into class and said good morning. When she asked about a cartoon he had seen, he remembered the parrot was in the cartoon. She told him that our minds sometimes mix up pictures, and that he had not been telling a lie.

Explain this in three short sentences.

Daniel had spent eight months on the grant application for his community-garden project in Porto. On Friday he clicked submit at 4:58 pm, two minutes before the deadline. The decision would take six weeks. That weekend he refreshed his email forty times. On Sunday, Beatriz found him rereading the budget table. "Did you do everything you could?" she asked. He thought. "I checked every number. I asked three people to review it. I got the letters of support." "Then what's left?" "Waiting." "And is waiting yours to do anything about?" He laughed, a bit tired. "No." Beatriz tossed him his swimming bag. "Then let's go to the sea." At the beach he still thought about the grant, but he didn't refresh anything. For six weeks he worked on the garden with the kids, grant or no grant.

Daniel submits his grant application just before the deadline and keeps checking his email. Beatriz asks what is left to do, and he admits only waiting remains, which he cannot control. They go to the sea, and for six weeks he keeps working on the garden.

It was after five o'clock when Sherlock Holmes left me, but I had no time to be lonely, for within an hour there arrived a confectioner's man with a very large flat box. This he unpacked with the help of a youth whom he had brought with him, and presently, to my very great astonishment, a quite epicurean little cold supper began to be laid out upon our humble lodging-house mahogany. There were a couple of brace of cold woodcock, a pheasant, a pate de foie gras pie with a group of ancient and cobwebby bottles. Having laid out all these luxuries, my two visitors vanished away, like the genii of the Arabian Nights, with no explanation save that the things had been paid for and were ordered to this address.

Explain this to a child in a few sentences.

Holmes goes out, and soon a man arrives with a big flat box and a young helper. They set out a fancy cold supper with birds, a pie and old bottles on the table. Then they leave without explaining, except to say that everything was already paid for.

Give me the instructions in this speech as three bullet points.

"There is but one thing to do. It must be done at once. You must put this piece of paper which you have shown us into the brass box which you have described. You must also put in a note to say that all the other papers were burned by your uncle, and that this is the only one which remains. You must assert that in such words as will carry conviction with them. Having done this, you must at once put the box out upon the sundial, as directed. Do you understand?"

- Put the paper into the brass box.
- Add a note saying that the other papers were burned by the uncle and that this one is the only one left.
- Then put the box out on the sundial straight away, as directed.

Condense this into a single sentence.

"Yes, that is what makes it amusing. Had they fixed on any other man it would have been nothing; but his perfect indifference and your pointed dislike make it so delightfully absurd! Much as I abominate writing, I would not give up Mr. Collins's correspondence for any consideration. Nay, when I read a letter of his, I cannot help giving him the preference even over Wickham, much as I value the impudence and hypocrisy of my son-in-law. And pray, Lizzy, what said Lady Catherine about this report? Did she call to refuse her consent?"
The speaker finds the whole situation amusing and says he enjoys Mr. Collins's letters even more than Wickham's, then asks Lizzy what Lady Catherine said about the report.

The Prajapati Manu had a son, O king, of the name of the Ikshwaku. Of that king, illustrious as Surya, were born a hundred sons. His tenth son, O Bharata, was named Dasaswa, and this virtuous prince of infallible prowess became the king of Mahismati. Dasaswa's son, O king, was a righteous prince whose mind was constantly devoted to the practice of truth and charity and devotion. He was known by the name of Madiraswa and ruled over the Earth as her lord. He was constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas as also of the science of arms. Madiraswa's son was the king named Dyutimat who possessed great good fortune and power and strength and energy.

List the family line in this passage as bullet points.

- Manu's son was Ikshwaku, who had a hundred sons.
- His tenth son, Dasaswa, became king of Mahismati.
- Dasaswa's son Madiraswa was a righteous king who studied the Vedas and weapons.
- Madiraswa's son was the powerful king Dyutimat.

Summarize this story in under 50 words.

"You want to know why I left the company? I'm Raghav. I was a junior engineer at a chemical plant. My manager told me to sign off a waste report that said the water going into the river was clean. It wasn't. I'd tested it myself. The village downstream, where Alka's family lives, uses that river. Everyone said, 'Just sign. It's normal. Everyone does it. You'll lose your job.' Even my father said it. I lay awake. I kept asking myself, what if it were my own family drinking that water? Their dignity, their health, isn't less than mine. So I didn't sign. I reported it properly to the pollution control board. I lost my job. It took me eight months to find another. I don't think I'm some saint. Most days I'm just ordinary. But on that one thing, I couldn't bend."

Raghav was told to sign a report saying river water was clean, but he had tested it and knew it was not. He refused and reported it to the pollution board. He lost his job and found another after eight months.

Please summarize Holmes's reasoning in two sentences.

"I have seen those symptoms before," said Holmes, throwing his cigarette into the fire. "Oscillation upon the pavement always means an affaire de coeur. She would like advice, but is not sure that the matter is not too delicate for communication. And yet even here we may discriminate. When a woman has been seriously wronged by a man she no longer oscillates, and the usual symptom is a broken bell wire. Here we may take it that there is a love matter, but that the maiden is not so much angry as perplexed, or grieved. But here she comes in person to resolve our doubts."

Holmes says that a woman who hesitates on the pavement outside usually has a matter of the heart, and that one who has truly been wronged tends to break the bell wire instead. So he thinks this visitor is puzzled or sad, not angry, and she then comes in.

Condense this extract into three sentences.

Eshaan, your mother says you kicked your school bag across the room today? Sit with your Chandrika Nani. When I was ten, in Ujjain, my teacher made me stand on the bench for talking, the whole period, while the others giggled. I didn't cry in school. I came home and threw my slate on the floor. It cracked. Then our dog Kalu came to lick my hand, and I pushed him away and shouted at him. My mother saw everything. She didn't shout back. She sat me down and said, "Who are you really angry with?" I said, "The teacher!" and burst into tears. Then I felt terrible about Kalu. I gave him my roti that night. The anger was from school. I had just brought it home, where it was safe to throw.

Chandrika Nani tells Eshaan about a day at ten when her teacher shamed her in front of the class. She went home and threw her slate and shouted at her dog, until her mother asked who she was really angry with and she cried. She says the anger belonged to school, and she had just taken it home, where it felt safe.

What happens in this? Answer in two sentences.

The rest of the evening brought her little amusement. She was teased by Mr. Collins, who continued most perseveringly by her side; and though he could not prevail with her to dance with him again, put it out of her power to dance with others. In vain did she entreat him to stand up with somebody else, and offered to introduce him to any young lady in the room. He assured her that, as to dancing, he was perfectly indifferent to it; that his chief object was, by delicate attentions, to recommend himself to her; and that he should therefore make a point of remaining close to her the whole evening. There was no arguing upon such a project. She owed her greatest relief to her friend Miss Lucas, who often joined them, and good-naturedly engaged Mr. Collins's conversation to herself.

Mr. Collins stays by Elizabeth's side all evening, so she cannot dance with anyone else, however much she begs him to find another partner. Only Miss Lucas gives her some relief by often joining them and talking to him.

How would you put this extract in one sentence?

I did not gain very much, however, by my inspection. Our visitor bore every mark of being an average commonplace British tradesman, obese, pompous, and slow. He wore rather baggy grey shepherd's check trousers, a not over-clean black frock-coat, unbuttoned in the front, and a drab waistcoat with a heavy brassy Albert chain, and a square pierced bit of metal dangling down as an ornament. A frayed top-hat and a faded brown overcoat with a wrinkled velvet collar lay upon a chair beside him. Altogether, look as I would, there was nothing remarkable about the man save his blazing red head, and the expression of extreme chagrin and discontent upon his features.
The visitor looks like a plain, heavy, pompous tradesman in rumpled clothes, and the only notable things about him are his bright red hair and his look of annoyance.

Condense this passage into three sentences.

Had Elizabeth's opinion been all drawn from her own family, she could not have formed a very pleasing picture of conjugal felicity or domestic comfort. Her father, captivated by youth and beauty, and that appearance of good-humour which youth and beauty generally give, had married a woman whose weak understanding and illiberal mind had very early in their marriage put an end to all real affection for her. Respect, esteem, and confidence had vanished for ever; and all his views of domestic happiness were overthrown. But Mr. Bennet was not of a disposition to seek comfort for the disappointment which his own imprudence had brought on in any of those pleasures which too often console the unfortunate for their folly or their vice. He was fond of the country and of books; and from these tastes had arisen his principal enjoyments. To his wife he was very little otherwise indebted than as her ignorance and folly had contributed to his amusement. This is not the sort of happiness which a man would in general wish to owe to his wife; but where other powers of entertainment are wanting, the true philosopher will derive benefit from such as are given.

Elizabeth's own parents do not show her a happy marriage. Mr. Bennet married a pretty, good-humoured young woman, but her weak mind soon destroyed his respect and trust. He now finds comfort in books and the countryside, and enjoys his wife only as a source of amusement.

Please summarize this in three bullet points.

When the head teacher announced at assembly in the Valencia school that the library would close at lunch to save staff hours, Pablo rolled his eyes so hard Emil could practically hear it. For a week he sighed through every lesson and answered teachers in one word, and on Wednesday he stuck a sign reading BOOKS ARE NOT A LUXURY on the library door. A teacher took it down and gave him a warning. "You're angry, fine," Emil said at the bus stop. "But right now you're just the guy with the sign." Pablo kicked a stone. "Nobody asked us. That's what I hate." So they asked. Over the weekend they collected signatures from 212 students and three teachers, and wrote a one-page letter suggesting older students could volunteer at the desk. On Monday Pablo read it at the school council, voice shaking a little. The head didn't say yes. She said, "Let's trial it for a month."

- Pablo was angry that the school library would close at lunch and protested with a sign, which got him a warning.
- His friend Emil helped him ask other students and teachers instead, and they wrote a letter suggesting older students could volunteer at the desk.
- Pablo read the letter to the school council, and the head agreed to a one-month trial.

Shrink this passage to two sentences.

Her inquiries after her sister were not very favourably answered. Miss Bennet had slept ill, and though up, was very feverish, and not well enough to leave her room. Elizabeth was glad to be taken to her immediately; and Jane, who had only been withheld by the fear of giving alarm or inconvenience, from expressing in her note how much she longed for such a visit, was delighted at her entrance. She was not equal, however, to much conversation; and when Miss Bingley left them together, could attempt little beside expressions of gratitude for the extraordinary kindness she was treated with. Elizabeth silently attended her.
Elizabeth learns that Jane slept badly and has a fever, so she goes straight to her room. Jane is delighted by the visit but too weak to talk much, so Elizabeth quietly looks after her.

I need the gist of this text in two sentences.

I then thought that my father would be unjust if he ascribed my neglect to vice or faultiness on my part, but I am now convinced that he was justified in conceiving that I should not be altogether free from blame. A human being in perfection ought always to preserve a calm and peaceful mind and never to allow passion or a transitory desire to disturb his tranquillity. I do not think that the pursuit of knowledge is an exception to this rule. If the study to which you apply yourself has a tendency to weaken your affections and to destroy your taste for those simple pleasures in which no alloy can possibly mix, then that study is certainly unlawful, that is to say, not befitting the human mind. If this rule were always observed; if no man allowed any pursuit whatsoever to interfere with the tranquillity of his domestic affections, Greece had not been enslaved, Caesar would have spared his country, America would have been discovered more gradually, and the empires of Mexico and Peru had not been destroyed.

The narrator now thinks his father was right to blame him, because a person should keep a calm mind and any study that weakens one's love for simple pleasures and family is wrong. He says that if this rule had always been followed, many great cruelties and conquests in history would not have happened.

Tell me in two sentences what this extract says.

We left Oxford with regret and proceeded to Matlock, which was our next place of rest. The country in the neighbourhood of this village resembled, to a greater degree, the scenery of Switzerland; but everything is on a lower scale, and the green hills want the crown of distant white Alps which always attend on the piny mountains of my native country. We visited the wondrous cave and the little cabinets of natural history, where the curiosities are disposed in the same manner as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. The latter name made me tremble when pronounced by Henry, and I hastened to quit Matlock, with which that terrible scene was thus associated.

The travellers leave Oxford for Matlock, where the hills remind the narrator of Switzerland though they are smaller and lack the Alps. When Henry mentions Chamounix, the narrator trembles at the memory and hurries to leave.

Explain what happens here to a child in simple words.

So Alice began telling them her adventures from the time when she first saw the White Rabbit. She was a little nervous about it just at first, the two creatures got so close to her, one on each side, and opened their eyes and mouths so very wide, but she gained courage as she went on. Her listeners were perfectly quiet till she got to the part about her repeating "You are old, Father William," to the Caterpillar, and the words all coming different, and then the Mock Turtle drew a long breath, and said "That's very curious."

Alice nervously tells two strange creatures about her adventures, starting from when she first saw the White Rabbit. She grows braver as she talks, and the Mock Turtle says it is very curious when he hears how the words came out wrong in her poem.

Summarize this text in three sentences.

So here's the funny part, looking back. In my first month at the firm, Pankaj sir barely said anything to me except things like "Fine" or "Send it by five." I decided he disliked me. Honestly, I was sure of it. So I, the only girl in that team, stopped talking in the huddles. I just nodded and took notes. Then at the end of the month he said to someone, not knowing I could hear, "Manjula doesn't seem very interested. Never asks anything." I was shocked. Not interested? I was terrified! And he wasn't disliking me, he was just like that with everyone, short and quick, because he had twelve projects. We'd each made up a story about the other. That's me, Manjula. Quiet does not mean bored, I learnt.

Manjula thought her new boss disliked her because he spoke so briefly, so she stopped speaking in team meetings. He, in turn, thought she was uninterested. In fact he was just busy with many projects, and she learned that being quiet does not mean being bored.

I see by your eagerness and the wonder and hope which your eyes express, my friend, that you expect to be informed of the secret with which I am acquainted; that cannot be; listen patiently until the end of my story, and you will easily perceive why I am reserved upon that subject. I will not lead you on, unguarded and ardent as I then was, to your destruction and infallible misery. Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow.

Explain what he is saying, for a child.

The speaker says he cannot share his secret yet, because he does not want his friend to suffer as he did. He wants his friend to learn from his example that chasing too much knowledge is dangerous, and that it is happier to be content with a small, familiar world.

The conversation soon turned upon fishing; and she heard Mr. Darcy invite him, with the greatest civility, to fish there as often as he chose, while he continued in the neighbourhood, offering at the same time to supply him with fishing tackle, and pointing out those parts of the stream where there was usually most sport. Mrs. Gardiner, who was walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look expressive of her wonder. Elizabeth said nothing, but it gratified her exceedingly; the compliment must be all for herself. Her astonishment, however, was extreme; and continually was she repeating, "Why is he so altered? From what can it proceed? It cannot be for me, it cannot be for my sake that his manners are thus softened. My reproofs at Hunsford could not work such a change as this. It is impossible that he should still love me."

What happens in this text? Use three sentences.

Elizabeth hears Darcy politely invite the man he is talking to to fish in his stream as often as he likes and offer him tackle. She is amazed by his changed manners. She wonders why he is so different and cannot believe it is for her sake.

We discerned Linton watching at the same spot he had selected before. My young mistress alighted, and told me that, as she was resolved to stay a very little while, I had better hold the pony and remain on horseback; but I dissented: I wouldn't risk losing sight of the charge committed to me a minute; so we climbed the slope of heath together. Master Heathcliff received us with greater animation on this occasion: not the animation of high spirits though, nor yet of joy; it looked more like fear.

One line only: what happens in this passage?

The narrator and her young mistress go back to meet Linton, and the narrator insists on climbing the slope with her; Linton greets them more eagerly than before, but he looks afraid rather than happy.

Summarize this reply in two sentences.

"Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument," said Holmes, taking the paper and glancing his eye down it. "This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it. The husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and the conduct complained of was that he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife, which, you will allow, is not an action likely to occur to the imagination of the average story-teller. Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example."

Holmes says the newspaper case is a poor example, because he has worked on it and knows that the husband was sober and faithful. The complaint was that he threw his false teeth at his wife after meals, which no ordinary storyteller would invent.

Explain this text in three short sentences.

Rashmi, you're leaving for Hyderabad next month, so listen to your Jeevan thatha for once. At nineteen I took the train from Mangalore to Bombay for a mill job. The first week was all noise and wonder. By the sixth week, nobody knew my name. The canteen rice was wrong, the fish was wrong, even the rain smelled wrong. I shared a room with five men from Bihar who were kind, but their jokes went over my head. At night I lay on my mat and cried into my towel so nobody would hear. I wrote to my amma that I wanted to come home. She wrote back, 'Come if you must. But wait till Deepavali first.' I waited. That crying didn't mean I had chosen wrong, kutty. It meant I loved where I came from. Both things were true.

Jeevan thatha tells Rashmi that at nineteen he moved to Bombay for work. He felt lonely, cried at night and wanted to go home. He says the crying meant he loved his old home, not that he had chosen wrong.

Can you tell this to a child in simple words?

My courage and perseverance were invigorated by these scoffing words; I resolved not to fail in my purpose, and calling on Heaven to support me, I continued with unabated fervour to traverse immense deserts, until the ocean appeared at a distance and formed the utmost boundary of the horizon. Oh! How unlike it was to the blue seasons of the south! Covered with ice, it was only to be distinguished from land by its superior wildness and ruggedness. The Greeks wept for joy when they beheld the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, and hailed with rapture the boundary of their toils. I did not weep, but I knelt down and with a full heart thanked my guiding spirit for conducting me in safety to the place where I hoped, notwithstanding my adversary's gibe, to meet and grapple with him.

A man felt braver after being mocked and kept crossing huge deserts until he saw the sea, which was icy and wild. Long ago people cried with joy at the sight of the sea, but he knelt and thanked his guiding spirit for bringing him safely to the place where he hoped to meet his enemy.

Summarize what happens in this meeting as bullet points.

At the panchayat meeting in Dhanauri, a seed dealer pointed to three farmers in the front row. "All three used our new wheat seed, and all three doubled their harvest!" Heads nodded. Shreya, the young agriculture extension worker, raised her hand. "How many farmers in the block bought this seed last season?" The dealer hesitated. "Around forty." "And the other thirty-seven?" Nazia, a farmer at the back, called out, "My field had the same seed. Half of it failed." Two more hands went up. Shreya kept her voice friendly. "Maybe it's a good seed. But before the panchayat praises it, let's hear from all forty, and check whose fields had canal water." The dealer's smile tightened. The three in the front row shifted in their seats.

- A seed dealer says three farmers doubled their harvest with his seed, as proof that it is good.
- Shreya asks how many farmers bought it, and Nazia says half of her field failed.
- Shreya suggests hearing from all forty buyers and checking who had canal water before praising the seed.

Give me a summary as bullet points.

He picked it up and gazed at it in the peculiar introspective fashion which was characteristic of him. "It is perhaps less suggestive than it might have been," he remarked, "and yet there are a few inferences which are very distinct, and a few others which represent at least a strong balance of probability. That the man was highly intellectual is of course obvious upon the face of it, and also that he was fairly well-to-do within the last three years, although he has now fallen upon evil days. He had foresight, but has less now than formerly, pointing to a moral retrogression, which, when taken with the decline of his fortunes, seems to indicate some evil influence, probably drink, at work upon him. This may account also for the obvious fact that his wife has ceased to love him."

- A man examining an object says its owner was clearly very intelligent.
- The owner was fairly well-off three years ago but has since fallen on hard times.
- He thinks the owner has become less careful about the future and may have turned to drink.
- That may be why the owner's wife no longer loves him.

Explain this to a child in simple words.

So she swallowed one of the cakes, and was delighted to find that she began shrinking directly. As soon as she was small enough to get through the door, she ran out of the house, and found quite a crowd of little animals and birds waiting outside. The poor little Lizard, Bill, was in the middle, being held up by two guinea-pigs, who were giving it something out of a bottle. They all made a rush at Alice the moment she appeared; but she ran off as hard as she could, and soon found herself safe in a thick wood.

Alice eats a cake and shrinks until she can slip out of the door. Outside, a crowd of little animals and birds waits, and the poor Lizard is being helped by two guinea-pigs. They all rush at her, so she runs away until she is safe in a thick wood.

Shorten this passage to under 50 words.

People ask me how the reading corner in our chawl started. I'm Sharmila, and honestly, it started with one borrowed book and a street light. I was twenty-four, working at a tailoring unit, sharing one room with four family members. I wanted to become a teacher someday, but that felt like a rich person's dream. One evening Minakshi, the girl from next door, asked me to read her a story. We sat on the steps under the light because there was no room inside. Next evening three kids came. Then eight. I wrote words on an old slate and we made up games. Two years on, I'm doing a distance diploma in teaching. I didn't wait to be ready. The steps were ready enough.

Sharmila started a reading corner in her crowded chawl by reading a story to a neighbour's child on the steps. More children joined, and now she is studying for a teaching diploma. She says she did not wait to feel ready.

Summarize this story in three short sentences.

In the small town of Sirsi, everyone knew when a family bought something new. When the Hegde family next door got a car, Deepak's mother mentioned it twice at dinner. When Sabina's colleague at the school went to Kerala for a holiday, the staff room talked about it for a week. So Deepak and Sabina bought a scooter on instalments, then a big fridge, then took a trip to Goa on the credit card. They never sat down to see if their two salaries, his at the cooperative bank and hers at the school, could carry it all. By the monsoon, the card bills were arriving faster than the salaries. They paid one card with another. The quarrels started small, about who had wanted the fridge. Then they happened almost every night. Their little son started going quiet whenever the phone rang. One evening Sabina sat on the step with the bills and simply cried.

Deepak and Sabina copied their neighbours and bought a scooter, a big fridge and a holiday on credit. They never checked whether their two salaries could pay for it all. Soon the card bills grew faster than their pay, they quarrelled every night, and their son went quiet.

Tell me in a single line what this extract says.

He then threw into the waters (of the sea) both the bow and the couple of inexhaustible quivers. After this, O chief of Bharata's race, the god of the fire disappeared then and there. The heroic sons of Pandu next proceeded with their faces turned towards the south. Then, by the northern coast of the salt sea, those princes of Bharata's race proceeded to the south-west. Turning next towards the west, they beheld the city of Dwaraka covered by the ocean.
After the fire god disappears, the Pandava brothers travel south and then west along the coast, where they see the city of Dwaraka covered by the sea.

What is happening here? Summarize it in two sentences.

Elizabeth, feeling it incumbent on her to relieve him from so unpleasant a situation, now put herself forward to confirm his account, by mentioning her prior knowledge of it from Charlotte herself; and endeavoured to put a stop to the exclamations of her mother and sisters, by the earnestness of her congratulations to Sir William, in which she was readily joined by Jane, and by making a variety of remarks on the happiness that might be expected from the match, the excellent character of Mr. Collins, and the convenient distance of Hunsford from London.

Elizabeth confirms Sir William's news, since she already knew it from Charlotte, and tries to stop her mother's and sisters' loud reactions by congratulating him warmly. She and Jane then praise the match, including Mr. Collins's good character and the convenient distance from London.

Sum up what Elizabeth says in one sentence.

"Be happy, my dear Victor," replied Elizabeth; "there is, I hope, nothing to distress you; and be assured that if a lively joy is not painted in my face, my heart is contented. Something whispers to me not to depend too much on the prospect that is opened before us, but I will not listen to such a sinister voice. Observe how fast we move along and how the clouds, which sometimes obscure and sometimes rise above the dome of Mont Blanc, render this scene of beauty still more interesting. Look also at the innumerable fish that are swimming in the clear waters, where we can distinguish every pebble that lies at the bottom. What a divine day! How happy and serene all nature appears!"

Elizabeth tells Victor to be happy and says she is content, although a small worry about the future whispers to her, and she points to the clouds, the clear water and the fish to show how beautiful the day is.

Condense this extract into a single sentence.

They very soon came upon a Gryphon, lying fast asleep in the sun. (If you don't know what a Gryphon is, look at the picture.) "Up, lazy thing!" said the Queen, "and take this young lady to see the Mock Turtle, and to hear his history. I must go back and see after some executions I have ordered;" and she walked off, leaving Alice alone with the Gryphon. Alice did not quite like the look of the creature, but on the whole she thought it would be quite as safe to stay with it as to go after that savage Queen: so she waited.
The Queen orders a sleeping Gryphon to take Alice to the Mock Turtle, then leaves to see about executions, and Alice decides it is safer to stay with the Gryphon.

Summarize this diary entry in two sentences.

Thursday THE RAIN CAME. First the sky went purple-grey, then the wind shook the drumstick tree, and then drops as big as coins hit the dust. The whole courtyard smelled of wet clay. I stood out in it with my mouth open, and Vasudha didi laughed at me from the doorway. Then I saw a long line of ants carrying eggs up the wall, all at once, as if someone had told them.
